Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on January 26, 2025
Review Body: Don’t waste your time or money on this book! It reads like a doctoral dissertation saying the same thing with repetition. Most of the message is common sense - keep your kids away from phones or screen time on other devices until at least high school, because it causes depression and anxiety. Keep them away from social media, pornography, etc. Get them outside to play more often and give them more in person social time. While these ideas are sound, the author makes it appear they are solely the reason for Gen Z distress and that is not the case. To imply it is is not reasonable. What is alarming is that although the author suggests that kids have more independence and get out of their rooms, he wants them to run errands alone in a day and age when you cannot do that for safety reasons. He also encourages helicopter parents, which negates a child having independence. The author also claims that lack of religion is to blame. While he claims that single parent and minority households have the most screen time, his generalizations are unfair. It makes the reader wonder if this author has children or even knows anyone in single parent or minority households. The book is primarily “scientific” information, graphs and generalizations that seem based more in opinion than facts. Angled to fit the author’s narrative. To find out if these generalizations were true, a large number of interviews were needed to see if it was the majority and it doesn’t appear those were done.

Review Body:
Parents have tried to remove all risk from their children's lives, even though a reasonable amount of risk is vital to proper development, and the world is actually safer today for children than it has been at any time in history.
On the other hand, children have substituted a virtual world for the real world, interacting through their cell phones with little or no supervision from parents, even though they are at much greater risk there.
Substituting virtual interaction for real interpersonal interaction during formative years (9-14) is harmful to a child's development and is irreversible, causing young adults to be more anxious and depressed. Parents should not allow children to have smartphones during this stage of their lives.
This thesis is intuitive, but it is examined in depth in the first chapter of the book. Every following chapter repeats the same message with the addition of some anecdotal and statistical evidence.

Review Body: I'll start by saying that I'm an avid reader. Very, very seldom is it that I don't finish a book that I've started. This is one book that I can't finish. It's awful. The author is right that cell phones, the internet, etc. are bad in many ways. Especially with young people. This book goes on and on and on about charts and graphs that tell us what common sense should already have told most people. The book is 295 pages up to the acknowledgements. I could only read to page 131. Where this book really set me off was at page 113 where the author compares people behavior with cat behavior. The author says that Edward Thorndike put hungry cats in "puzzle boxes". The hungry cats would "thrash around" trying to escape to get food but couldn't get out until performing a particular behavior. What the h---??!! Sounds like Thorndike should be put in a puzzle box instead of innocent cats! It makes me wonder where the money comes from for these idiotic tests and these charts. Probably tax payer money. I'm tearing off the cover to burn and then throwing the book into the recycle trash bin where it belongs.
